questions.q: The Reaction Quotient ($Q​$) differs from the Equilibrium Constant ($K​$) because:
options: $Q​$ is calculated using equilibrium concentrations only.
$Q​$ is calculated using concentrations at any point in time, not just equilibrium.
$Q​$ uses addition instead of multiplication in the expression.
questions.explain: $Q​$ has the same form as $K​$ but is calculated using current concentrations/partial pressures, which may or may not be at equilibrium.
questions.subject: Chemistry

questions.q: For the reaction $A \rightleftharpoons B$, if $Q_c = 10$ and $K_c = 5$, in which direction will the reaction proceed to reach equilibrium?
options: The reaction will proceed to the right (towards products).
The reaction will proceed to the left (towards reactants).
The system is already at equilibrium.
questions.explain: Since $Q > K$, the ratio of products to reactants is too high. The reaction must shift to the left (reactants) to decrease $Q​$ until it equals $K​$.
questions.subject: Chemistry

questions.q: Consider: $2\text{NOCl}(g) \rightleftharpoons 2\text{NO}(g) + \text{Cl}_2(g)$. If a mixture contains reactants and products such that $Q < K$, what will happen to the partial pressure of $\text{Cl}_2$ as equilibrium is approached?
questions.explain: If $Q < K$, the reaction proceeds in the forward direction to produce more products. Therefore, the partial pressure of the product $\text{Cl}_2$ will increase.
questions.subject: Chemistry

questions.q: A reaction vessel contains a mixture where the Reaction Quotient $Q​$ is exactly equal to the Equilibrium Constant $K​$. This implies:
options: The reaction is spontaneous in the forward direction.
The reaction is spontaneous in the reverse direction.
The system is at equilibrium and no net change will occur.
The limiting reactant has been consumed.
questions.explain: When $Q = K$, the system satisfies the equilibrium condition; the rates of forward and reverse reactions are equal, and no net change occurs.
questions.subject: Chemistry

questions.q: For the reaction $\text{H}_2(g) + \text{I}_2(g) \rightleftharpoons 2\text{HI}(g)$, $K_c = 50$. A mixture is prepared with $[\text{H}_2] = 1M$, $[\text{I}_2] = 1M$, and $[\text{HI}] = 5M$. What is $Q_c$ and the direction of shift?
questions.explain: $$Q_c = \frac{[\text{HI}]^2}{[\text{H}_2][\text{I}_2]} = \frac{5^2}{1 \times 1} = 25$$. Since $K_c = 50$ and $Q_c = 25$, we have $Q < K$. The reaction shifts right (forward).
questions.subject: Chemistry

questions.q: Which combination of parameters is required to calculate the reaction quotient $Q_p$ for a gaseous reaction?
options: Instantaneous partial pressures of all species.
questions.explain: $Q_p$ is calculated using the partial pressures of reactants and products at a specific instant in time.
questions.subject: Chemistry

questions.q: In a precipitation reaction, the reaction quotient is often called the Ion Product ($IP$). If $IP > K_{sp}$, what is observed?
questions.explain: If the Ion Product ($Q​$) exceeds the Solubility Product ($K_{sp}$), the solution is supersaturated and the excess ions will precipitate out until $Q = K_{sp}$.
questions.subject: Chemistry

questions.q: For an exothermic reaction, if the temperature is increased, the equilibrium constant $K​$ decreases. If the concentrations remain instantaneous unchanged immediately after heating, how does $Q​$ compare to the new $K​$?
questions.explain: Instantaneous concentrations (and thus $Q​$) haven't changed yet. However, $K​$ has decreased ($K_{new} < K_{old}$). Since $Q​$ was equal to $K_{old}$, now $Q > K_{new}$. The system will shift left.
questions.subject: Chemistry
